home.title: Your county, out in the open.
home.intro: Report a problem, follow every shilling, and vote on what your ward builds next. From any phone.

wardCard.trustHint: 40% how fast reports are answered, 35% projects finished, 25% budgets kept.

home.phoneBody: Dial {code} on any phone to report a problem, check a case, vote or get alerts. No data bundles needed.
home.trustBody: You never need to give your name. We keep the ward, the category and your description. Public pages only ever show totals.
home.moneyBody: See what each ward was promised, what has been spent, and who is doing the work.
home.loopBody: Every report goes to a named department with a deadline. If the deadline passes, it climbs to a supervisor, and the overdue count goes on this page for everyone to see.

report.title: Report a problem
report.intro: Tell {county} County what is broken. It takes about a minute. You do not need to give your name.
report.addPhotoHint: Optional. Up to 3 photos. We remove location details from photos before they leave your phone.
report.category: What kind of problem is it?
report.categoryHelp: Pick the closest one. An officer will check it.
report.sensitiveNote: This kind of report is sent to the county's integrity desk, not to the department it is about.
report.urgentNote: This is treated as urgent. If someone is in danger right now, call 999 or 112 first.
report.describePlaceholder: For example: A big pothole on the road next to the market. Matatus are swerving into oncoming traffic.
report.describeHelp: Please do not include names or phone numbers. We remove them anyway.
report.callbackBody: Optional. If you add your number we will text you when the status changes. It is stored separately from your report and never shown publicly.
report.callbackConsent: Yes, text me updates about this report.
report.callbackInvalid: Enter a Kenyan mobile number, like 0712 345 678.
privacyBullets: Your name is never asked for.
Photos are stripped of GPS and phone details on your device.
Public pages only show totals by ward and category.
The case reference is safe to share. It shows status, never your details.

pulse.title: County Pulse
pulse.intro: How the county is really doing, in the open. Live figures on responsiveness, delivery and participation. Only totals are shown: never names, never who reported what.
pulse.trustFormula: 40% how fast reports are answered, 35% projects finished, 25% budgets kept.
pulse.leagueSub: Higher is better. Based on the last 90 days.
pulse.channelSub: Share of reports by channel, last 90 days
pulse.demoNote: Sample figures shown until the county's database is connected.

how.title: How it works
how.intro: One county, one system, many ways in. Whatever you use, your report or vote lands in the same place and follows the same rules.
how.channelsTitle: Four ways to reach the county
how.webBody: Use this site on any phone. Install it to your home screen and it works even with weak signal: reports wait on your phone and send when you are back online.
how.ussdBody: Dial {code} on any phone. Choose your ward, then report, vote, check a case or get alerts. No data bundles needed.
how.smsBody: Text your report to {code}. We reply with a case reference and tell you when its status changes.
how.voiceBody: Call the county line and speak in English or Swahili. Your message is written down and handled like any other report.
how.ladderIntro: Rules, not moods, decide who is told and when. If a deadline passes, the case climbs, and the overdue count is shown publicly.

ladder.d2: Not acknowledged: a reminder, and their supervisor is copied
ladder.target: Deadline missed: the chief officer is told, and the overdue counter goes up
ladder.targets: Each type of problem has its own deadline
ladder.late30: 30 days late: the CEC member and the Assembly committee, by name
ladder.monthly: Every month: a digest to the Auditor-General and Controller of Budget

how.ladderNote: Artificial intelligence helps to sort and summarise reports. It never decides who gets escalated, and it never approves anything.
how.privacyIntro: Reporting is anonymous by design. Voting needs a phone check, so it is kept completely separate from reports.
weKeepList: The ward, category and description of your report.
A case reference and its status history.
Photos, with location and phone details removed on your phone before upload.
If you ask for SMS updates: your number, stored separately and never shown publicly.
weNeverList: Ask for your name on a report.
Show your number, or anything that identifies you, on any public page.
Join your votes to your reports.
Let artificial intelligence make a decision about you.
how.rightsBody: Under the Data Protection Act you can ask what we hold about you, ask for corrections, or ask us to delete it. Write to the county's Data Protection Officer or dial {code}.
how.accessBody: English and Kiswahili, large text, high contrast, a simple mode for slow phones, and every action available without a smartphone.

open.title: Open County
open.intro: Who gets paid, how they were chosen, and which patterns deserve a closer look. Built only from public tender and project records. A flag is a reason to look, never proof of wrongdoing.

who.title: Who wins county money
who.intro: Share of awarded value by supplier. In a healthy market no single supplier dominates.
who.none: No tenders have been awarded yet.

conc.title: How concentrated is the market?
conc.hint: The index adds up each supplier's squared share of value. Below 1,500 is competitive, above 2,500 is highly concentrated.

how.title: How contracts are awarded
how.intro: Open tendering lets anyone compete. Other methods have real uses but should stay the exception.
how.single: Awarded with one bidder or none
how.avgDays: Average days a tender stays open

watch.title: Automated watch
watch.intro: Every award and project is checked against published rules, every day. Each flag shows its reason, and the county can publish a response next to it.
watch.none: Nothing stands out right now. The checks keep running.

method.title: How the checks work
method.intro: We follow the open-contracting approach used in Ukraine, Chile and Colombia: plain rules over public data, published so anyone can check them.
rules: One supplier holds 25% or more of awarded value (40% or more is high priority)
One supplier won four or more awards and a fifth of all awards
Three suppliers hold 60% or more of awarded value
30% or more of awarded value skipped open tendering
A supplier's awards were mostly direct or restricted
A quarter or more of awarded tenders had one bidder or none
A supplier won two or more tenders with a single bidder
Three or more awarded tenders were open for under a week
An award is more than 15% above the estimate (30% is high priority)
Three awards to one supplier for the same work in the same place within 30 days
A supplier holds awards while its last tax compliance check was negative
A project has spent more than 10% over budget, or is stalled after spending half
method.disclaimer: A flag is a prompt to look closer. There are often good reasons, such as emergencies or specialised work. Nobody is accused of anything here.

nowItems: Report a problem with a photo and a map pin, from any phone

faq.a1: No. Reporting, voting, alerts and following projects work without one. An account is for county services, payments and your own dashboard.
faq.a2: Yes. We keep the ward, category, description and photos, never your name. A phone number for a callback is optional and kept apart from the report.
faq.q3: How fast will the county respond?
faq.a3: Each kind of report has a target to acknowledge and a target to fix, shown on this page. When a deadline passes the case climbs to a supervisor and the overdue count is published.
faq.a4: Overdue cases go up to a ward or sub-county administrator, then to the chief officer, then to the County Assembly. Overdue counts are public for every ward.
faq.a5: You confirm your phone once with a code. One vote per person per round, counted by ward. Your vote is stored as a scrambled code, never with your number.
faq.q6: I do not have a smartphone.
faq.a6: Dial {code} on any phone to report, check a case, vote or get alerts. No data bundles needed.
faq.a7: A pattern in public tender data that deserves a closer look, such as one supplier winning a large share. It is never an accusation, and the county can publish a response.
faq.q8: Who can see what I do?
faq.a8: Public pages show totals only. Staff see only what their role needs, and every staff action goes into an audit trail that cannot be edited.

api.title: Open data for journalists and researchers
api.intro: The county's tenders and awards, published as Open Contracting Data Standard (OCDS) releases. Free to use with credit, no key needed.
api.f1: Tender: reference, title, sector, ward, estimated value, method, bidding period, number of bidders
api.f3: Buyer and publisher, and a stable identifier (ocid) for each procurement
api.limit: Up to 500 releases per request. Use limit and offset to page.

voice.unsupported: Voice typing is not available in this browser. Type your report instead.
voice.error: We could not hear that. Try again or type.

dominant_supplier.title: {name} holds {share}% of awarded value
dominant_supplier.why: One supplier holding more than a quarter of awarded value is a common reason to look at how work is being shared.

repeat_winner.title: {name} won {wins} awards, {share}% of all
repeat_winner.why: Winning many awards can be legitimate, and is also what repeated favouritism looks like. Worth checking the tenders were competitive.

top3_concentration.title: Three suppliers hold {share}% of awarded value
top3_concentration.why: A market this concentrated leaves little competitive pressure on price and quality.

non_competitive_share.title: {share}% of awarded value skipped open tendering
non_competitive_share.why: Direct and restricted procurement have legitimate uses, such as emergencies, and should stay a small share.

contractor_direct_reliance.title: {name}: {nonopen} of {wins} awards were not openly tendered
contractor_direct_reliance.why: Most of this supplier's awards came through direct or restricted procurement.

single_bidder_share.title: {share}% of awarded tenders had one bidder or none
single_bidder_share.why: A single bidder cannot show that the price was tested.

contractor_single_bid.title: {name} won {count} tenders with a single bidder
contractor_single_bid.why: Winning several tenders where nobody else bid deserves a look at how they were advertised.

short_tender_period.title: {count} awarded tenders were open for under a week
short_tender_period.why: Very short tender periods limit who can respond in time.

award_above_estimate.title: {name} was awarded at {pct}% of its estimate
award_above_estimate.why: A large gap between estimate and award can mean a poor estimate or a price that was not tested.

split_awards.title: {name} received {count} awards for the same work within 30 days
split_awards.why: Several awards for the same kind of work in the same place can indicate a larger job split up to stay under a threshold.

kra_noncompliant.title: {name} failed its last tax compliance check
kra_noncompliant.why: Public bodies are expected to award only to tax compliant suppliers.

project_overrun.title: {name} has spent {pct}% of its budget
project_overrun.why: Spending above budget should come with an approved variation and a public explanation.

stalled_after_spend.title: {name} is stalled after {pct}% of its budget was spent
stalled_after_spend.why: Money has left but work has stopped. Residents should be told why and when it will resume.

project_late.title: {name} is {days} days past its expected date
project_late.why: The project has not reached completion by the date the county published.
